string-array.name: whats_new_items
string-array.item: New (beta): “Import from audio” recognizes an audio file on the device, such as a voice message, and turns it into a draft. It needs the recognition pack from Settings.

New look: Home shows the dish of the day large, the cookbook (formerly “Collection”) is a list with tabs at the top and a home icon, a recipe has tabs for ingredients, instructions and notes, and Add is its own page.

Clearer dough calculator: the result stays at the top, values change with minus and plus, the preferment is highlighted, and tapping biga, poolish, sourdough starter or a yeast type explains the term.
Settings as a list with icons: switches for the most important options (“Quick”) sit at the top, and each group opens as its own view.

New “Storage” section in Settings: it shows how much space the app uses – split into app, photos, thumbnails, recipes, language pack, recognition pack, translations and cache, plus the total. Packs and the cache can be deleted there.

Dough schedule: for pizza and bread the dough calculator creates a schedule (for example biga 1 to 3 days in the refrigerator). In the recipe, “Start dough” begins the process; the app shows where the dough stands and when to continue, also on Home.
Compact dough calculator: values sit side by side, the preset takes less room, and the bar at the bottom also shows the preferment for biga or poolish.
Tidier settings: groups can be expanded and collapsed, so everything fits on one screen.
While cooking, the text for ingredients and steps is a little larger.
Tags when importing: the category and keywords of a recipe page appear in the draft as suggestions to tap; tags come back with a recipe file.
Cooking: “Large text for cooking” in the ⋮ menu of the recipe view enlarges ingredients, steps and notes. Notes can now be added right in the recipe view with “Add note”.
Sorting the collection: The new icon next to search switches between “Title A–Z” and “Recently added”. Umlauts and accents sort with their letter, and the choice is remembered.
Recipe view: The photo now extends up behind the top bar.

Voice input while cooking: The new microphone button in the cooking bar listens for “Next”, “Previous”, “Repeat”, “Read aloud” and “Stop”; “Microphone off” ends listening. This needs the recognition pack from Settings once.
Headset buttons: In Settings under “Read aloud”, choose what the play/pause, next and previous buttons do while cooking. This also covers headsets that convert gestures themselves.
Dough calculator: every value has a slider with a number you can tap and type; the “Numbers | Sliders” switch is gone, plus and minus remain only for small whole numbers.
“Default 250 g” with “To default” appears only when a value differs from its default.
The cooking bar shows “Step 2 of 5”, “Next” is emphasized, and the current step has a bar at its edge. With large text the buttons stand in two rows.
The photo in the recipe view is lower so ingredients and steps start earlier.

string-array.name: privacy_paragraphs
string-array.item: Recipes, photos and notes are stored only on this device. There is no account, no advertising, no tracking and no sharing with third parties.

The app only goes online on request: for “Import from link” and when downloading the language pack for translation or the recognition pack for voice input. For “Import from link” it loads exactly that one page and, if available, its photo. As with any browser, the page learns the device’s internet address (IP address), the time and the preferred language. No cookies are stored and no details about the device are sent.
Otherwise content only leaves the device when it is shared or backed up. Notes are never shared. The backup file is not encrypted.
The language pack and the recognition pack for voice input come from the project page on GitHub. GitHub learns the device’s internet address (IP address) and the time. No recipes are sent.

The microphone is only needed for voice input in the cooking view and for dictating a recipe, and is only requested when it is tapped for the first time. It only listens while the button is on (when dictating: until “Done”) and the screen is on. Audio files chosen for “Import from audio” stay unchanged and are not stored. Recognition runs entirely on the device; nothing is recorded, stored or sent.
Text recognition, translation and voice input run entirely on the device, without internet. Android’s automatic cloud backup is turned off.

Preferment: Part of the flour, water and yeast is mixed ahead of time. This gives more flavor and a lighter dough.
Biga: Stiff preferment with little water.
Poolish: Liquid preferment with as much water as flour.
Sourdough starter: Flour and water, fermented without added yeast. Yeast can still be added to the final dough.
Salt, oil and hydration in % of flour
Check the entries marked in red.
Do not eat raw dough. Raw flour can contain germs.
All numbers are rough guides, not standards. Flour, room temperature and oven change the result.

More water makes many doughs softer and stickier and can favor a more open crumb; less water gives a firmer dough that is usually easier to shape. Hydration is the water as a percentage of the total flour; flour and water of a preferment count too.

Rough guide: many white breads about 60 to 70 %, very wet doughs such as ciabatta or focaccia around 80 %, Neapolitan pizza about 56 to 62 %. Pan pizza varies widely by recipe (about 55 to 80 %). Rye, whole grain and other special doughs differ clearly.
How much water a dough takes up depends on flour, grind, handling and the consistency wanted. Wet doughs are harder to shape; it is better to change the value in small steps.
Salt improves flavor, strengthens the dough structure and slows yeast fermentation somewhat. Without salt a dough often turns slack and the bread bland.

For many yeast breads, about 1.8 to 2.2 % of the total flour is a useful starting point (sources also give 1.5 to 2.5 %). For Neapolitan pizza, the quantities given by the pizza makers’ association work out to about 2.8 %.
Too much salt can make the dough tighter, slow the yeast more and taste salty. The right value depends on the recipe and how the dough is handled.

Oil can make the crumb more tender and change how well the dough stretches. The effect depends on the amount, when it is added and the rest of the recipe; how long bread stays fresh also depends on recipe and storage.
Rough guide: bread mostly 0 to 5 %, pan pizza and very soft doughs up to about 10 %. Solid fats such as butter act differently from oil.
Very large amounts can change the dough structure noticeably. It is better to raise the amount step by step.

Amount of yeast, temperature and rising time together decide how fast the dough ripens. More yeast makes it rise faster; less yeast with a longer rising time can favor flavor, but this is no guarantee.

A long rising time at refrigerator temperature (several hours up to a few days) needs clearly less yeast than a short rising time at room temperature. Fresh, instant and active dry yeast differ in strength; the calculator converts when the type changes (approximate).

Cold slows fermentation but does not stop it: the dough keeps ripening in the refrigerator. Too short gives little flavor, too long makes the dough slack and sour. How long a dough stays usable depends on yeast, salt, flour and temperature. The time is only a guide: the dough should visibly grow.
A preferment can improve flavor and dough properties; biga tends to make the dough firmer, poolish more extensible. Flour and water of the preferment count toward the totals in the calculator.
Biga is typically stiff (about 50 to 60 % water of its flour), poolish liquid (about 100 %). About 20 to 50 % of the total flour in the preferment is common.

Ripening time depends on temperature: a biga usually needs 8 to 16 hours at about 15 to 20 °C. Left too long, the preferment collapses and smells sharply sour. Biga and poolish are made with yeast and are not sourdough; with sourdough, the yeast in the final dough is optional.
A stiff preferment with little water. It gives stronger flavor, an open crumb and a dough that stretches well. Typical for Italian pizza and ciabatta.
About 50 to 60% water of the flour in the preferment, usually 20 to 40% of the total flour and very little yeast (about 0.1 to 1% of the preferment flour).
At about 59 to 68°F (15 to 20°C) usually 8 to 16 hours, in the refrigerator up to three days. Too long makes the dough slack and sour.
A liquid preferment of equal parts flour and water. It gives a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a very light crumb. Typical for baguettes and rolls.
About 100% water of the flour in the preferment, plus 0.05 to 0.5% yeast of the preferment flour.
Usually 8 to 16 hours at room temperature. It is ripe when the surface is full of bubbles and starts to sink.
A starter of flour and water with wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria. It leavens the dough and adds acidity and flavor.
Usually 10 to 30% of the total flour as starter.
Needs much longer rising times than yeast, often 8 to 24 hours, and the starter has to be fed regularly.
Pressed yeast of living yeast cells, the cube from the refrigerated shelf. It is the reference for converting the other yeast types.
1 g fresh yeast equals about 0.33 g instant yeast and about 0.4 g active dry yeast.
Store cold and keep only a few weeks. Dissolve in lukewarm liquid or crumble finely.
A fine powder that is mixed straight into the flour. It is stronger than fresh yeast.
About one third of the amount of fresh yeast.
Keeps for a long time unopened; once opened store cool and dry.
Coarser granules that are dissolved in lukewarm water before use.
About 40% of the amount of fresh yeast, so a little more than instant yeast.
Dissolve in water of about 95°F (35°C) until foamy.
